Maximum total length in Gag (Mycteroperca microlepis) has been documented at 145 centimeters [Li = 145 centimeters], a size that places this species among the larger members of the genus within the Gulf of Mexico. Such an ultimate length is achieved only after many years of sustained growth, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic investment before the onset of reproductive activity. Newly hatched individuals emerge from pelagic eggs at a remarkably diminutive size, with the wet weight at birth estimated at 0.00019 grams [Wwb = 0.00019 grams], a value consistent with the small egg diameters typical of serranid fishes. This minuscule starting mass necessitates a highly fecund reproductive strategy to offset the immense mortality pressures experienced during the planktonic larval phase. The transition from a pelagic larva to a benthic juvenile involves a dramatic metamorphic climax, after which growth rates begin to decelerate as the fish approaches its asymptotic dimensions. Field surveys targeting large adults in the northeastern Gulf have confirmed that individuals exceeding 130 centimeters are exceptionally rare, suggesting that the species experiences elevated natural mortality near its maximum recorded size.

Sexual maturation in Gag is closely tied to body size rather than chronological age, with the total length at puberty estimated at 58 centimeters [Lp = 58 centimeters]. This size threshold marks the point at which vitellogenesis onset and spermiation onset become physiologically possible, though first spawning may be delayed further by social or environmental factors. Histological examinations of gonadal tissue have revealed that fish below this length invariably possess immature, undifferentiated gonads, whereas individuals exceeding 58 centimeters commonly exhibit active gametogenesis. The species functions as a protogynous hermaphrodite, wherein most individuals mature first as females and later undergo sexual inversion to become male at larger sizes, a pattern that further complicates the relationship between length, age, and reproductive status. Comparisons with congeneric species such as Mycteroperca bonaci indicate that a puberty length of 58 centimeters is relatively late, reflecting the slow maturation pace of this long-lived predator. The energetic demands of reaching this size are substantial, requiring efficient prey capture strategies throughout the juvenile phase.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the maximum reproductive output of Gag has been assessed by examining both fecundity per event and spawning frequency. The daily egg production rate can be estimated from the fact that females release approximately 11,780 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 11,780 eggs per spawning event] and are capable of undertaking 1 spawning event each year [F_R_i = 1 spawning event each year], yielding roughly 32 eggs per day. This annual spawning rhythm synchronizes with the spring phytoplankton bloom in the Gulf of Mexico, ensuring that pelagic larvae encounter favorable feeding conditions at the onset of exogenous feeding. The high fecundity per event compensates for the substantial egg and larval mortality inherent in a broadcast spawning strategy. Thermal conditions at 24 °C are close to the optimum for gamete viability and embryonic development in this subtropical serranid, as temperatures much lower than this significantly reduce fertilization success and hatching rates observed in experimental trials.

Adult body mass provides a complementary perspective on size, with the ultimate wet weight recorded at approximately 4,270 grams [Wwi = approximately 4,270 grams] in the largest verified individuals. This mass corresponds closely to predictions derived from the length-weight relationship for the species, reinforcing the value of 145 centimeters [Li = 145 centimeters] as a reliable upper bound for total length. The transformation from a yolk-sac larva weighing just 0.00019 grams to a mature adult exceeding 4 kilograms represents a mass increase of over seven orders of magnitude, an ontogenetic trajectory that demands a prolonged period of active feeding growth. Maximum adult body mass in females tends to be slightly lower than in males, a dimorphism attributable to the energetic costs of egg production. Comparisons with other epinephelines indicate that a wet weight of 4,270 grams is moderate for a fish of this length, suggesting a relatively streamlined body morphology suited for ambush predation in reef environments. The ability to sustain such a large body mass depends on access to productive foraging grounds throughout the continental shelf.

Longevity records for Gag, derived from otolith annulus counts and tag-recapture studies conducted at 24 °C [T = 24 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 4,015 days [am = approximately 4,015 days], equivalent to about 11 years. This lifespan places the species at the shorter end of the range for large epinephelines, likely reflecting the high metabolic demands of a warm-water existence and elevated predation risk on juveniles. The age-related death of senescent adults occurs after a relatively compressed reproductive window, given that the pubertal length of 58 centimeters [Lp = 58 centimeters] may not be attained until several years of age. Population models suggest that fishing pressure, particularly on the large, male-dominated size classes, can severely truncate the lifespan distribution, with wild individuals rarely surviving past 8 years in exploited areas. The interplay between a birth mass of 0.00019 grams [Wwb = 0.00019 grams] and a lifespan of 4,015 days highlights the extreme demographic vulnerability of this species: high early mortality must be offset by high fecundity per event and annual spawning to maintain population stability under natural conditions.
